summary: Explains how the IPsec security services apply to IP multicast packets, which the base IPsec architecture mainly describes for unicast. It matters only to IPsec implementations that support multicast. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec protects traffic between two devices, and its architecture assumes a single destination address. Multicast is different: one packet goes to a group, so many receivers share one key. This document extends IPsec for that case, adding the databases and the key handling a group needs, and a tunnel mode that keeps the packet looking like multicast on the network.

subtitle: How IPsec protects packets sent to a whole group, where the destination is a multicast address.

tldr.problem: The IPsec architecture mainly defines security associations between two devices, but multicast packets have a group destination address and many receivers sharing the same keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds optional extensions to RFC 4301: group databases (GSPD and GPAD), group security associations set up by a group key management protocol, tunnel mode with address preservation, and a re-key rollover scheme.
tldr.outcome: IPsec devices that support multicast can protect IP multicast packets and keep them routable as multicast. Devices that do not support multicast need not implement the extensions.

today: RFC 5374 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 4301 and matters only to IPsec implementations that support multicast.

sections.title: Scope of the Multicast Extensions
sections.content:
The Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol, RFC 4301, provides security services for traffic at the IP layer and describes an architecture for IPsec-compliant systems. Those services primarily describe security associations shared between two IPsec devices, typically with traffic selectors that include a unicast address in the IP destination field, and they result in an IPsec packet with a unicast address in that field.

The same services can also be used to tunnel IP multicast packets, where the tunnel is a pairwise association between two IPsec devices. RFC 4301 defined manually keyed transport mode IPsec SA support for IP packets with a multicast address in the destination field, but it did not define the interaction of an IPsec subsystem with a Group Key Management protocol, nor the semantics of a tunnel mode IPsec SA with an IP multicast address in the outer IP header. This document fills those gaps.

It describes OPTIONAL extensions to RFC 4301 that further define the IPsec security architecture so that groups of IPsec devices can share SAs. In particular, it supports SAs with traffic selectors that include a multicast address in the IP destination field and that result in an IPsec packet with an IP multicast address in that field, and it describes additional semantics for IPsec Group Key Management subsystems. The term GKM protocol is used generically, so no particular protocol is assumed. An IPsec implementation that does not support multicast is not required to support these extensions, and RFC 4301 semantics remain unchanged by their presence unless stated otherwise.

The extensions support SAs that result in IPsec packets with IPv4 or IPv6 multicast group addresses as the destination, and both Any-Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast group addresses are supported. They are used when management policy requires that IP multicast packets protected by IPsec remain IP multicast packets; when policy instead requires the packets to be encapsulated as IP unicast packets, these extensions are not used. The extensions also support SAs with IPv4 broadcast addresses and IPv6 anycast addresses, because these destination types share many of the characteristics of multicast addresses: there may be several candidate receivers of a packet protected by IPsec.

The IPsec architecture makes no requirements on entities that do not participate in IPsec, such as the network devices between IPsec endpoints, so these multicast extensions do not require intermediate systems in a multicast-enabled network to participate in IPsec. No requirement is placed on the use of multicast routing protocols such as PIM-SM or on multicast admission protocols such as IGMP, and all implementation models of IPsec are supported.

This version of the specification requires that all IPsec devices participating in a security association be homogeneous: they MUST share a common set of cryptographic transform and protocol-handling capabilities. The semantics of an IPsec composite group, a heterogeneous group formed from the union of two or more sub-groups, is left for future standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions are optional and only matter to devices that implement multicast. They cover group security associations where several devices share keys, the tunnel mode that keeps the protected packet a multicast packet, and how a device decides that it is allowed to join a group in the first place.

sections.title: Overview of IP Multicast Operation
sections.content:
IP multicasting is a way of sending a single packet to a host group, a set of zero or more hosts identified by a single IP destination address. IP multicast packets are delivered to all members of the group either with best-effort reliability or as part of a reliable stream, for example the NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast protocol in RFC 3940.

A sender to an IP multicast group sets the destination of the packet to an IP address allocated for IP multicast. Potential receivers join the group by registering with a network routing device, signalling their intent to receive packets sent to that group.

Network routing devices configured to pass IP multicast packets take part in multicast routing protocols such as PIM-SM. Those protocols maintain state about which devices have registered to receive packets for a given multicast group. When a router receives an IP multicast packet, it forwards a copy of the packet out of each interface for which there are known receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: In multicast, one packet carries a group address as its destination and every router in the path forwards copies of it to the interfaces where receivers have joined. That is why the IPsec extensions have to keep the protected packet's addresses matching the ones the multicast routers expect.

sections.title: Tunnel Mode with Address Preservation
sections.content:
IPsec supports two modes of use. In transport mode, the IP Authentication Header and the Encapsulating Security Payload provide protection primarily for next layer protocols; in tunnel mode, they are applied to tunneled IP packets. A host implementation using these multicast extensions MAY use either mode to encapsulate an IP multicast packet, with processing rules identical to those of RFC 4301, except that the destination address of the IPsec packet is an IP multicast address rather than a unicast host address. A security gateway implementation MUST use a tunnel mode SA, in particular because it needs tunnel mode to encapsulate incoming fragments, since IPsec cannot directly operate on fragments.

New header construction semantics are needed when tunnel mode encapsulates IP multicast packets that are to remain IP multicast packets, and the document calls this tunnel mode with address preservation.

When a host or router receives an IP multicast packet, the destination address of the packet is compared to the local IP multicast state. If the outer destination address of an IP multicast packet were set to another IP address, the receiving host or router would not process it properly. The security gateway therefore has to populate the multicast IP destination address in the outer header with the destination address from the inner header, after IPsec tunnel encapsulation.

IP multicast routing protocols typically create multicast distribution trees based on the source address as well as the group address. If the security gateway populated the outer source address of an IP multicast packet with its own IP address, the resulting IPsec-protected packet could fail the Reverse Path Forwarding checks performed by other routers, and a failed check can result in the packet being dropped. To accommodate those checks, the security gateway SHOULD populate the outer IP address from the original packet's IP source address. A gateway that preserves the source address will not receive ICMP Path MTU or other messages intended for the gateway, so applications that need those messages should not ask for source address preservation.

Destination address preservation and source address preservation are separate, and are described as attributes in the Group Security Policy Database and copied into the corresponding Security Association Database entries. Address preservation applies only to tunnel mode IPsec SAs where the IP version of the encapsulating header is the same as that of the inner header. When the IP versions differ, IP multicast packets can be encapsulated using a tunnel interface, as described in RFC 4891, where the tunnel is also treated as an interface by the multicast routing protocols.

In summary, propagating both the IP source and destination addresses of the inner IP header into the outer tunnel header allows IP multicast routing protocols to route a packet properly when the packet is protected by IPsec. That is what makes it possible for a host or a security gateway to provide IPsec services for IP multicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gateway protects a multicast packet with IPsec, it wraps it in an outer IP header. Normally that outer header carries the gateway's own address, which breaks multicast routing. Tunnel mode with address preservation copies the inner source and destination addresses into the outer header, so the packet still looks like the same multicast packet to every router on the way.

sections.title: The Group Databases: GSPD, SAD and GPAD
sections.content:
The Group Security Policy Database supports both unicast security associations as defined by RFC 4301 and the multicast extensions, and is considered to be the SPD with the multicast semantics added. It gains an address preservation flag with two attributes: AP-L, used in the processing of the local tunnel address, and AP-R, used in the processing of the remote tunnel process. AP-L set to true means the inner IP header source address is copied to the outer IP header source address during tunnel mode header construction, and AP-R means the inner destination address is copied to the outer destination address.

The GSPD also gains a directionality attribute, because an IP multicast address must not be sent as the source address of an IP packet. Where a unicast SPD entry swaps its Local and Remote addresses and ports during incoming checks, an SPD entry with a remote IP multicast address does not swap them. Directionality can be one of three types: symmetric, meaning a pair of SAs is created, one in each direction; sender only, meaning one SA is created in the outbound direction; and receiver only, meaning one SA is created in the inbound direction. Sender-only and receiver-only entries SHOULD support multicast IP addresses in their destination address selectors. If the requested processing is BYPASS or DISCARD and the type is sender only, the entry MUST be put in the outbound GSPD only, and reciprocally a receiver-only entry MUST go to the inbound GSPD only.

The outbound GSPD MUST implement a policy action capability that triggers a GKM protocol registration exchange, so that group keying can happen as the application starts. A Group Sender policy might trigger on a match with a specified multicast application packet entering the implementation on the protected interface, or emitted on the protected side toward the unprotected interface; the registration exchange then sets up the outbound SAD entry that encrypts the data stream. At the Group Receiver endpoints, the IPsec subsystem MAY use GSPD policy that initiates a registration exchange, for example on detecting a device in the protected network joining a multicast group that matches policy, such as by receiving an IGMP or MLD join group message on a protected interface. The subsystem MAY also provide policy that initiates a de-registration exchange, which lets the key server reduce the exposure of the group's secret key by re-keying on a membership change; a Group Member does not de-register until it detects that there are no more receivers behind a protected interface.

The Security Association Database entry says whether tunnel or transport mode applies, and is amended so that when tunnel mode is specified it also says whether address preservation is applied to the outer IP header. Address preservation MUST NOT be specified when the IP version of the encapsulating header and that of the inner header do not match, and the local address, the remote address or both MAY be marked as preserved.

The Group Peer Authorization Database is a new data structure, analogous to the PAD of RFC 4301, that links the GSPD to the GKM subsystem. It identifies the GCKS, or group of GCKS devices, authorized to communicate with this IPsec entity; specifies the protocol and method used to authenticate each GCKS; provides the authentication data for each GCKS; constrains the traffic selectors that a GCKS may assert when creating SAs; and constrains the types and values of Group Identifiers for which a GCKS may provide group policy. It is not consulted by IKE or other authentication protocols that do not act as GKM protocols.

Each GPAD entry holds one or more GCKS Identifiers, the authentication protocol, for example GDOI or GSAKMP, the authentication method, for example certificates or pre-shared secrets, and the authentication data. For certificate-based authentication the entry may also help with checking revocation, through a pointer to a CRL repository or the name of an OCSP server. The entry also holds the constraints the Group Member applies to the policy it receives.

The Group Identifier is an opaque byte string of IKE ID type Key ID that identifies a secure multicast group. It MUST be at least four bytes long and less than 256 bytes long, and other IKE ID types MAY be supported. Each GKM registration exchange MUST use the asserted ID to locate an identity in the GPAD, and the entry supplies the authentication method and data used to verify the asserted identity before any group policy is accepted. Before presenting a Group Identifier to the GCKS, the Group Member checks that the entry for the authenticated GCKS includes that Group Identifier. When IPsec SA policy arrives, each data flow is compared with the data flows in the GPAD entry: policy that matches is accepted, policy that does not match is discarded, and the reason SHOULD be recorded in the audit log.
sections.plainLanguage: Three databases hold the group's rules. The GSPD says which traffic is protected and in which direction, and adds two flags for address preservation. The SAD holds the live security associations. The GPAD is new: it names the key servers this device trusts, how to authenticate them, and which groups and traffic they are allowed to configure.

sections.title: Group Security Associations and Re-Key Rollover
sections.content:
An IPsec implementation supporting these extensions supports a number of security associations: one or more IPsec SAs plus one or more GKM SAs used to download the parameters that create the IPsec SAs. Together these are called a Group Security Association, as described in RFC 3740.

Several IPsec group security associations can exist concurrently for two reasons. There may be several Group Senders authorized in the group, each with its own IPsec SA maintaining anti-replay state, although a group that does not rely on IP security anti-replay services can share one SA for all of its Group Senders. And the life spans of a Group Sender's two or more IPsec SAs are allowed to overlap in time, so that there is continuity in the multicast data stream across group re-key events, which is called re-key rollover continuity. The re-key continuity rollover algorithm depends on an IPsec SA management interface between the GKM subsystem and the IPsec subsystem, and the IPsec subsystem MUST provide mechanisms for the GKM subsystem to add and delete IPsec SAs.

Two timer parameters govern the algorithm. The Activation Time Delay defines how long after the start of a re-key event to activate the new IPsec SAs, expressed in seconds. It is typically set to the maximum time it takes to deliver a multicast message from the GCKS to all of the group's members, and it is a GKM group policy parameter that SHOULD be configurable at the Group Owner management interface on a per group basis. The Deactivation Time Delay defines how long after the start of a re-key event to deactivate those IPsec SAs destroyed by the re-key event, also in seconds. Its purpose is to minimize the residual exposure of the group's keying material after a re-key event has retired that material. It is independent of the IPsec SA soft lifetime attribute, and if a GKM subsystem does not implement it, other group security policy mechanisms MUST determine when to deactivate an IPsec SA.

Each group re-key multicast message sent by a GCKS signals the start of a new Group Sender IPsec SA time epoch, and each epoch has an associated set of two IPsec SAs. The GCKS periodically multicasts a Re-Key Event message to the group, which may contain group policy directives, new IPsec SA policy and group keying material. In the absence of a reliable multicast transport, the GCKS may re-transmit the RKE a policy-defined number of times to improve availability, and the GKM subsystem starts the ATD and DTD timers after it receives the last retransmission.

The GKM subsystem interprets the RKE to configure the group's GSPD and SAD with the new IPsec SAs. Each SA that replaces an existing SA is called the leading edge SA, and it has a new Security Parameter Index and the keying material that keys it. For a period of ATD seconds after the RKE is multicast, the Group Sender does not yet transmit data using the leading edge SA, while other Group Members prepare by installing the leading edge SAs into their GSPD and SAD. After the ATD period, the GKM subsystem directs the Group Sender to begin transmitting with the leading edge SA, with its data encrypted by the new keying material, and only authorized Group Members can decrypt those transmissions.

The trailing edge SA is the oldest security association in use by the group for that sender. All authorized Group Members can receive and decrypt data for it, but the sender does not transmit new data with it after it has moved to the leading edge SA, and the group's GKM subsystems delete it after the DTD period has elapsed since the RKE transmission. This strategy lets the group drain in-transit datagrams while the transition happens, and staggering the roles of the SAs improves synchronization even when propagation delays are high.

Whether the transition between epochs provides forward and backward secrecy is a group policy decision, enforced by the re-key protocol's keying material and algorithm. Implementations MAY offer a Group Owner management interface option to enable or disable re-key rollover continuity for a particular group. The specification requires that a GKM and IPsec implementation MUST support at least two concurrent IPsec SAs per Group Sender as well as the re-key rollover continuity algorithm.

Finally, the GKM subsystem is often introduced alongside an existing IPsec subsystem as a companion to IKEv2. Both the GKM protocol and IKEv2 must be able to share access to a common GSPD and SAD, and the mechanisms that give them mutually exclusive access to those structures are a local matter, including the GSPD-O and GSPD-I caches. IKEv2 SPI allocation is entirely independent from GKM SPI allocation, because group security associations are qualified by a destination multicast IP address and may optionally have a source IP address qualifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A group re-keys by sending a multicast message with the new key. Receivers must install the new key before the sender starts using it, and the old key must survive long enough for packets already in the network to arrive. Two timers do this: the activation delay before the new key is used, and the deactivation delay before the old key is dropped.

sections.title: Data Origin Authentication
sections.content:
Data origin authentication is a security service that verifies the identity of the claimed source of data. A Message Authentication Code is often used to achieve it for connections shared between two parties. Typical MAC authentication methods that use a single shared secret are not sufficient for groups with more than two parties: with a MAC algorithm, every Group Member can use the MAC key to create a valid MAC tag, whether or not it is the authentic originator of the group's data.

Where the property of data origin authentication is required for an IPsec SA shared by more than two parties, an authentication transform in which the receiver is assured that the sender generated the message should be used. Two possible algorithms are Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication, described in RFC 4082, or RSA digital signature, described in RFC 4359.

In some cases, for example with digital signature authentication transforms, the processing cost of the algorithm is significantly greater than that of a hashed MAC method. To protect against denial-of-service attacks from a device that is not authorized to join the group, the IPsec SA using this algorithm may be encapsulated with an IPsec SA using a MAC authentication algorithm. Doing so requires the packet to be sent across the IPsec boundary a second time for additional outbound processing on the Group Sender, and a second time for inbound processing on Group Receivers. This use of AH or ESP encapsulated within AH or ESP accommodates the constraint that AH and ESP define an integrity check value for only a single authenticator transform.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared secret cannot prove who sent a message in a group, because every member could produce a valid tag. Where the group needs to know which member sent a packet, it uses a per-sender signature or a broadcast authentication scheme such as TESLA instead.

sections.title: IP Traffic Processing
sections.content:
Processing of traffic follows Section 5 of RFC 4301, with the additions described here when the multicast extensions are supported.

Outbound, if an IPsec SA is marked as supporting tunnel mode with address preservation, either or both of the outer header source or destination addresses are marked as preserved. The tunnel mode header construction rules of RFC 4301 are amended: if address preservation is not marked for either the outer IP header source address or the destination address, those addresses identify the endpoints of the tunnel, the encapsulator and the decapsulator. If address preservation is marked for the source address, it is copied from the inner IP header source address, and if it is marked for the destination address, it is copied from the inner IP header destination address. The inner addresses identify the original sender and recipient of the datagram from the perspective of this tunnel. Address preservation MUST NOT be marked when the IP version of the encapsulating header and that of the inner header do not match.

Inbound, an IPsec device supporting these multicast extensions may, depending on its GSPD policy, populate an outer tunnel header with a destination address such that the packet is not addressed to an IPsec device, and it therefore has to accept and process IP traffic that is not addressed to it. For compatibility with RFC 4301, a packet is taken to be addressed to the device if it has a unicast destination address belonging to the system itself, or if it is a multicast packet received by the system itself; multicast packets not received by the device are not considered addressed to it.

Where a packet appears to be IPsec protected and is addressed to this device, or appears to be IPsec protected and is addressed to a multicast group, an attempt is made to map it to an active SA via the SAD. A new step handles destination address preservation: if the packet is addressed to a multicast group and AH or ESP is specified as the protocol, the packet is looked up in the SAD using the SPI plus the destination, or the SPI plus the destination and source addresses. If there is no match, the packet is directed to an SPD-I lookup. The document notes that if the device is a security gateway and the SPD-I policy is to BYPASS the packet, a subsequent security gateway along the routed path of the multicast packet may decrypt it.

One further rule applies when address preservation is in use: the marked addresses in the outer IP header MUST be verified to be the same values as in the inner IP header. If the addresses are not consistent, the IPsec system MUST discard the packet and treat the inconsistency as an auditable event.
sections.plainLanguage: On the way out, the outer header is built from the inner one when address preservation is set. On the way in, a packet addressed to a multicast group is looked up in the security association database by its SPI and group address, and if the outer and inner addresses disagree the packet is dropped and logged.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The multicast extensions build on the unicast-oriented IP security architecture of RFC 4301, and inherit many of its security considerations. The document lists the issues the extensions solve, the issues they leave open, and the deployment matters that affect security.

The service provides confidentiality using a group shared encryption key; group source authentication and integrity protection using a group shared authentication key; Group Sender data origin authentication using a digital signature, TESLA or another mechanism; anti-replay protection for a limited number of Group Senders using the ESP or AH sequence number facility; and filtering of multicast transmissions identified with a source address of systems that group policy does not authorize to be Group Senders, using the IPsec stateless firewall service. To support these, the definitions of the SPD, PAD and SAD databases are enhanced to allow automated group key management of large-scale cryptographic groups.

What is not solved: as in RFC 4301, it is out of scope to defend the group's keys or its application data against attacks that target vulnerabilities of the operating environment in which the IPsec implementation runs, and the risk of attacks from an adversary in the network is magnified because the group keys are shared across many systems.

Outsider attacks are the case of an adversary outside the group who can launch a multicast flooding denial-of-service attack against the group from a system whose IPsec subsystem does not filter unauthorized multicast transmissions; who has compromised a multicast router and can corrupt or delete all multicast packets destined for the group endpoints downstream of that router; or who has captured a copy of an earlier multicast packet transmission and replayed it to a group that does not have the anti-replay service enabled. For a large-scale any-source multicast group it is impractical for the Group Receivers to maintain anti-replay state for every potential Group Sender, so group policies that require anti-replay protection for such a group should consider an application layer multicast protocol that can detect and reject replays.

Insider attacks start with a member admitted to the group by the GKM system. A cryptographic group holds shared secrets entrusted to all members, so the service's security guarantees are no stronger than the weakest member admitted, and the GKM system is responsible for responding to a compromised member by running a re-key procedure that expels it and distributes new keying material, or by terminating the group. Once an adversary is in, it can disclose the secret group key or the group data to an unauthorized party, though methods such as traitor tracing or watermarking can help the forensics and are outside the scope of the document. It can forge packet transmissions that appear to come from a peer Group Member, against which the group policy can require the data origin authentication service. And if that service uses digital signatures, the adversary can launch a computational resource denial-of-service attack by multicasting bogus signed packets.

Three deployment issues also matter. The service cannot defend against a poorly considered group security policy that allows a weaker cryptographic algorithm simply because all of the group's endpoints are known to support it, and large-scale groups can be difficult to upgrade to the current best algorithms; composite groups that straddle heterogeneous groups are one possible approach, and a standard solution for heterogeneous groups is an activity for future standardization, while in the interim a group's cryptographic capabilities could be synchronized with a secure and scalable software distribution management tool. Large-scale groups may also span several legal jurisdictions that limit cryptographic algorithms or key strengths, while the service as defined requires a single group policy per group, which remains an area for future standardization. Finally, the source IP address of a Source-Specific Multicast Group Sender can change during a group's lifetime, for example because of NAT, a mobility-induced change in the care-of-address, or a multi-homed host using a new interface, and the change makes GSPD entries out of date; in the worst case the sender's data from a new source address could be BYPASS processed by a security gateway and leak the group's data, so it is recommended that SSM secure multicast groups have a default DISCARD policy for all unauthorized Group Sender source IP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions give a group confidentiality, integrity, source authentication and some filtering. They do not stop an outsider flooding the group, an insider who has joined from forging traffic, or a weak algorithm chosen because every member happens to support it.
